820.title: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
820.hook: the first person to speak in the Gita is not Krishna or Arjuna. it's Duryodhana, talking to his old teacher.
820.tomorrow: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
820.howItsDone: The first chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is recited along with the rest, and the conches named in it, such as Krishna's Panchajanya, are familiar from pictures of Krishna and Arjuna in the chariot.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Bhishma Parva opened in a dark room: a blind king refused sight, and Sanjaya told him everything. Your line: a listener who chose to hear rather than see.
screen: `THE KING CHOSE TO HEAR.` · `SANJAYA TELLS IT ALL.`

segments.voice: Ask someone how the Bhagavad Gita begins, and they may tell you about Arjuna's doubt, or Krishna's teaching. But after the old king's question, the first real speech belongs to someone else. Duryodhana walks over to Drona, the teacher who trained the princes on both sides, and starts talking. He names the great fighters on the other side. Then he names his own. It sounds like a general's briefing. Listen closer, and it sounds like a man reassuring himself. Session two of six: the noise before the silence.
screen: `WHO SPEAKS FIRST?` → `DURYODHANA, TO HIS TEACHER` → `THE NOISE BEFORE THE SILENCE`

segments.voice: Duryodhana stands before Drona and points across the field. Look at the Pandava army, he says, arrayed by your own student, Drupada's son. He's reminding his teacher, a little sharply, that the enemy commander learned from him too. Then he lists his own champions, with Bhishma at their head, and tells everyone to guard Bhishma. Bhishma doesn't answer in words. To cheer Duryodhana, the old grandsire roars like a lion and blows his conch shell. Then the field erupts: conches, drums and horns from the Kaurava side. And from the other side, Krishna blows his conch, Panchajanya. Arjuna blows his, Devadatta. Bhima blows a huge one, and the rest of the Pandava fighters join in. The Gita says that sound tore at the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons and made the earth and sky resound. Hold that noise in your ears. Arjuna lifts his bow and asks Krishna to drive the chariot out between the two armies, so he can see who he's about to fight. Krishna sets it down right in front of Bhishma and Drona. And Arjuna looks. Grandfathers. Teachers. Uncles. Brothers. Sons. Friends. His limbs give way. His bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand. He sits down in the chariot and sets his weapons aside. After all that sound, the first chapter ends with a man sitting still. That stillness is where Krishna's teaching begins.
screen: `DURYODHANA BRIEFS DRONA` · `BHISHMA'S CONCH, THEN EVERY CONCH` · `THE CHARIOT BETWEEN THE ARMIES` · then, large: `ARJUNA SITS DOWN`

segments.voice: Whatever is busy around you or in your head, you don't need to quiet it. Breathing out, let your feet go still, then with each breath your knees, your hands, your shoulders, your jaw, until you've sat down in the middle of the noise, the way Arjuna did between the armies. If you pray, you can begin your prayer from that stillness.
Bhishma Parva. The book named for the grandsire, whose conch started the noise that ends in Arjuna's silence.
Your line: a man sitting still. All those conches, and the Gita begins with a bow set down. Until tomorrow.

821.title: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
821.hook: between two armies, a warrior asks his charioteer to be his teacher, and the charioteer smiles.
821.carry: I am your disciple, teach me
821.tomorrow: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
821.howItsDone: The second chapter of the Gita, where Arjuna becomes Krishna's disciple, is read and recited on its own and as part of the Bhishma Parva; paintings of the scene show Krishna teaching from the driver's seat.

segments.voice: Yesterday the conches roared, and Arjuna sat down in his chariot with his bow at his feet. Your line: a man sitting still.

A chariot stands alone in the open ground, with an army on either side, waiting. The warrior in it is a great archer, and he has just put his bow down. The man holding the reins is his cousin and his friend, who agreed to come to this war without picking up a single weapon. Back in the Udyoga days, Arjuna chose Krishna that way, unarmed. Now the choice pays off in a way no one planned. Session three of six: the moment a soldier becomes a student.
screen: `A CHARIOT BETWEEN TWO ARMIES` → `THE DRIVER CARRIES NO WEAPON` → `A SOLDIER BECOMES A STUDENT`

segments.voice: At the start of the Gita's second chapter, Krishna first tries a soldier's language. Shake off this weakness, he says. Stand up. It doesn't work. Arjuna answers with questions. How can he shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, men he should be honoring? Better to live as a beggar than to eat food stained with their blood. He doesn't even know which would be worse: winning or losing. Then he says the line that changes everything. I am your disciple. Teach me. I've come to you for refuge. He tells Krishna plainly that he will not fight, and falls silent. Notice where this happens. Not in a forest hermitage, not in a quiet room with a lamp, but in the open, between two armies, with a teacher who is also the driver. And the text gives a small detail here: Krishna, as if smiling, begins to speak. What he says first is startling to a man who has just refused to kill his family. You grieve for those you shouldn't grieve for. There was never a time when I was not, nor you, nor these kings, and there will never be a time when we cease to be. The body is worn and cast off, the way a person puts away old clothes. What's real in each of them cannot be killed. Read in place, this lands differently. It isn't a seminar on the soul. It's an answer to one terrified man, about particular people standing across the field: his grandfather, his teacher, his kin.
screen: `STAND UP: A SOLDIER'S WORDS FAIL` · `I AM YOUR DISCIPLE. TEACH ME.` · `KRISHNA, AS IF SMILING` · then, large: `WHAT'S REAL CANNOT BE KILLED`

segments.voice: Let your breath be the reins: steady, not tight. Bring to mind a question you haven't been able to answer on your own, and don't solve it; breathing in, let it be there, and breathing out, let yourself be its student for a while. If you pray, you can bring that question into your prayer.
Bhishma Parva. The book of the battle where, before a single arrow flies, a soldier asks to be taught.
Your line: I am your disciple, teach me. The great archer's first step is to ask. Day eight hundred twenty-one, done.

822.title: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
822.hook: Krishna says he taught this teaching to the sun long ago, and Arjuna, his cousin, objects: you were born after the sun.
822.carry: better your own duty, done imperfectly
822.tomorrow: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
822.howItsDone: The Gita's third and fourth chapters, on action without attachment and on Krishna's coming age after age, are read and recited both on their own and as part of the Bhishma Parva.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna said, I am your disciple, teach me, and Krishna, as if smiling, began to speak. Today the student pushes back.

Families have a way of keeping each other honest. Tell a story about yourself at a holiday dinner, and someone who grew up with you will say: that's not how it happened. Something like that happens in the middle of the Gita. Krishna mentions, almost in passing, that he taught this same teaching long ago, to the sun. And Arjuna, his cousin, stops him. Wait. Your birth came later. The sun was born long before you. How could you have taught him? Session four of six: the argument in the chariot.
screen: `FAMILY KEEPS YOU HONEST` → `I TAUGHT THIS TO THE SUN` → `WAIT: YOU WERE BORN AFTER HIM`

segments.voice: Read in place, Arjuna is not a polite student. He pushes back like a soldier who needs an answer before the fighting starts. At the start of the third chapter he says, more or less: if you think understanding is better than action, why push me into this terrible action? You're confusing me. Tell me one thing for certain. Krishna doesn't send him off to think in a cave. No one can stay free of action, he says, even for a moment. Your nature moves you whether you like it or not. So act, but don't act for the prize. Act as an offering. He points to King Janaka, who reached the goal through action. He points to himself: there's nothing I need, and yet I keep working, because the world follows what the great ones do. Then a line that cuts close for Arjuna: better your own duty, done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Arjuna's duty, as a warrior, is standing across the field from him. Then the fourth chapter, and the moment from the hook. When Arjuna objects that Krishna was born after the sun, Krishna doesn't laugh it off. Many births have passed for both of us, he says. I know them all, and you don't. Whenever dharma fails and its opposite rises, I come into being, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma right. This is where the cousin in the driver's seat begins to show Arjuna who he is. And it happens because Arjuna argued.
screen: `WHY PUSH ME INTO THIS ACTION?` · `NO ONE CAN STAY FREE OF ACTION` · `BETTER YOUR OWN DUTY, IMPERFECT` · then, large: `I KNOW MY BIRTHS. YOU DON'T.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open and think of one small, ordinary task waiting for you. Breathing in, see yourself doing it; breathing out, let go of how it turns out: the praise, the result, whether anyone notices. If you pray, that task can be your offering.
Bhishma Parva. The book where a soldier argues with his teacher in the middle of a battlefield, and the argument opens the door.
Your line: better your own duty, done imperfectly. Not someone else's, done well, but yours. See you tomorrow.

823.title: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
823.hook: Arjuna is given a divine eye to see Krishna's universal form, and among the faces rushing into it are names the blind king knows.
823.tomorrow: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
823.howItsDone: The vision of the universal form in the Gita's eleventh chapter is read and recited, and it appears in temple art and paintings showing Krishna with many faces and arms before Arjuna's chariot.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna argued that Krishna was born after the sun, and Krishna answered: I know my births, and you don't. Your line: better your own duty, done imperfectly.

Two people in this story are given eyes they weren't born with. One is Sanjaya, who sees the whole battlefield from the palace so he can tell the king. The other is Arjuna, who in the eleventh chapter of the Gita asks to see Krishna as he truly is, and is told his ordinary eyes can't do it. So Krishna gives him a divine eye. And then there's us, listening, because the one describing Arjuna's vision is Sanjaya, speaking to a blind father. Session five of six: the vision, heard from inside the palace.
screen: `EYES THEY WEREN'T BORN WITH` → `ARJUNA GETS A DIVINE EYE` → `SANJAYA TELLS THE BLIND KING`

segments.voice: Arjuna sees a form with countless faces and eyes, a light like a thousand suns rising at once, the whole universe gathered in one body. In the Gita it's Sanjaya who says this to Dhritarashtra. Then the vision turns. Arjuna sees the warriors of the war rushing into terrible mouths, like rivers racing to the sea, like moths into a flame. And he names them. The sons of Dhritarashtra. Bhishma. Drona. Karna. Our own warriors too. Now hear it from where the king sits. He refused to watch this war. He asked only to be told. And here, in the middle of a teaching about God, Sanjaya tells him his own sons are among the faces disappearing into those mouths. Arjuna, shaking, asks: who are you? Krishna answers: I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds. Even without you, none of these warriors will survive. They are already slain by me. Be only the instrument. Then he names them again: Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha, Karna. Read alone, this chapter is a vision of the divine. Read in place, it's also a forecast, spoken over the heads of real men standing in their ranks, waiting. Bhishma is one of them; the book named for him has already told us he will fall. At the end, Arjuna, terrified, asks to see his friend's familiar face again. Krishna takes his gentle form, and Arjuna says: now I'm myself again.
screen: `A THOUSAND SUNS AT ONCE` · `THE WARRIORS RUSH INTO THE MOUTHS` · `I AM TIME. BE THE INSTRUMENT.` · then, large: `THE FAMILIAR FACE AGAIN`

segments.voice: Let your gaze go soft and widen your attention for a breath or two: the room, the building, the street, the sky over it. Then come back, gently, to one familiar thing near you, a cup, a chair, your own breath, and stay there. Arjuna saw everything and then asked for the familiar face; both are allowed, and if you pray, your prayer can rest there too.
Bhishma Parva. The book whose grandsire stands in the ranks while Arjuna's vision names him among those Time has already taken.
Your line: now I'm myself again. After the vision of Time, a friend's face was enough. That's day eight hundred twenty-three.

824.title: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
824.hook: the Gita is over, Arjuna has picked up his bow, and Yudhishthira takes off his armor and walks toward the enemy.
824.howItsDone: In the Mahabharata, the Gita is followed directly by Yudhishthira's unarmed walk to Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Shalya to ask their blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna saw the universal form, heard Bhishma named among the fallen, and asked for his friend's familiar face. Your line: now I'm myself again.

The teaching ends. Arjuna tells Krishna his confusion is gone and he will do as Krishna says. He picks up his bow. Both armies roar. And then, before a single arrow flies, Yudhishthira does something strange. He takes off his armor. He lays down his weapons. He climbs out of his chariot and walks, on foot, straight toward the enemy lines. His brothers run after him, asking where he's going. The other army starts to murmur that he's come to surrender. Session six of six: what the Gita leads into.
screen: `ARJUNA PICKS UP HIS BOW` → `YUDHISHTHIRA TAKES OFF HIS ARMOR` → `WALKING TOWARD THE ENEMY`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira walks to Bhishma, bows to him, and asks his permission to fight him, and his blessing. Read that right after the Gita. Krishna has just taught that a warrior must do his duty. Here is a man about to do exactly that: fight his grandfather, and honor him first. Bhishma is moved. In Ganguli's telling, he says that if Yudhishthira had not come to him like this, he would have cursed him with defeat. Instead he blesses him: fight, and win. Then he says something painfully honest about himself. A person is a slave to wealth, but wealth is no one's slave. I am bound to the Kauravas by their wealth. Ask me for anything except to fight on your side. So Yudhishthira asks a harder question. How can you be beaten in battle? No one can defeat me now, Bhishma tells him, and the time of my death has not yet come. Ask me again another time. Yudhishthira goes on to his teachers, Drona and Kripa, and to his uncle Shalya, and does the same with each. Then, standing between the armies, he calls out: anyone who chooses us, we'll choose them. And one of Dhritarashtra's own sons, Yuyutsu, crosses the field to the Pandava side. That's how the Gita sits in its place. It ends, and the very next thing is a man walking unarmed into the enemy's ranks, to honor the people he must fight.
screen: `HE BOWS AND ASKS A BLESSING` · `BHISHMA: I'M BOUND BY THEIR WEALTH` · `HOW CAN YOU BE BEATEN? ASK AGAIN` · then, large: `YUYUTSU CROSSES OVER`

segments.voice: Think of someone you're at odds with, a little or a lot, and for one minute picture yourself setting down whatever you carry against them, the way Yudhishthira set down his armor. Breathing in, see their face; breathing out, find one thing in them you can honestly respect, and stay with it. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Bhishma Parva. The book of the grandsire who blesses his opponent, confesses what binds him, and says: ask me again.
Your line: ask me again another time. A blessing given to the man who would fight him, and an answer kept for later. Until tomorrow.

825.title: Bhishma's fall
825.hook: the Kaurava commander loves the men he is fighting, and Duryodhana's friend Karna refuses to fight under him.
825.carry: a man who dies only when he chooses
825.howItsDone: Bhishma's terms as commander, Karna's refusal to fight under him, and the boon that lets him choose his death are told in the Mahabharata's Udyoga, Adi and Bhishma books, and are familiar parts of retellings of the war.

segments.voice: Yesterday Yudhishthira walked unarmed to Bhishma for his blessing, and the grandsire told him: ask me again another time.

An army might want a commander who hates the enemy. Duryodhana's commander doesn't. When Duryodhana asked Bhishma to lead his forces, in the Udyoga book, the old man said yes, and then set terms. The sons of Pandu, he said, are as dear to me as you are. I will fight their armies for you. I will not kill them. And there was a second problem, standing right there in the hall: Karna. Today, Bhishma's fall begins, with the strange shape of the side he leads.
screen: `A COMMANDER WHO DOESN'T HATE` → `HIS TERMS: NOT THE FIVE BROTHERS` → `AND KARNA IN THE HALL`

segments.voice: Start with Karna. Bhishma and Karna don't get along. In the Udyoga book, when Bhishma ranks the warriors on his own side, he rates Karna low, and Karna is stung. So when Bhishma takes command, Karna makes a vow of his own. As long as Bhishma lives, Karna will not fight. When Bhishma falls, then he'll take the field against Arjuna. So the Kaurava side goes into battle with its commander holding back from the five brothers, and Karna sitting in his tent. Now add something the epic told us long ago. When Bhishma was young, he gave up his claim to the throne and swore never to marry, so his father could marry again. In return, the epic says, his father gave him a gift: death would not take him until he chose it. Put those together and you have the riddle of the next days. Bhishma can't be beaten, and he won't be hurried. In the first day's fighting, the losses fall hard on the Pandava side. Uttara, the young prince of Virata, who held the reins for Arjuna in the cattle raid, is killed. So is his brother Shveta, at Bhishma's own hand. The family that sheltered the Pandavas pays first. So hold Bhishma's fall as a question, not just an event. How do you bring down a man who loves you, who can't be beaten, and who decides for himself when he dies? The epic takes its time answering.
screen: `KARNA WON'T FIGHT WHILE BHISHMA LIVES` · `THE BOON: DEATH WHEN HE CHOOSES` · `VIRATA'S SONS FALL FIRST` · then, large: `HOW DO YOU BRING HIM DOWN?`

segments.voice: Think of a commitment you carry, a job, a promise, a family role, that sometimes pulls against what you'd rather do. Breathing in, feel its weight honestly; breathing out, notice what in you still chooses to keep it, and let both be true, the way Bhishma held two loyalties on the same field. If you pray, you can bring that commitment with you.

826.title: Bhishma's fall
826.hook: Krishna promised not to fight. Then he jumps down from the chariot and runs at Bhishma, and Bhishma welcomes him.
826.carry: to be killed by you would be an honor
826.howItsDone: The scene of Krishna leaping from the chariot toward Bhishma, and Bhishma welcoming him, is told in the Bhishma book of the Mahabharata and appears in paintings and retellings of the war.

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma's fall began as a riddle: a commander who loves the other side, Karna waiting in his tent, and a man who dies only when he chooses.
screen: `A RIDDLE, NOT YET A FALL.` · `DEATH WHEN HE CHOOSES.`

segments.voice: A charioteer's work is the reins. Krishna came to this war with one promise: he would not take up a weapon. He drives the chariot, he talks, and in the Gita he taught. But he doesn't fight. Then, early in the battle, Bhishma is cutting through the Pandava ranks, and Arjuna is holding back. And Krishna leaps down from the chariot and runs at Bhishma on foot. Today: the day the driver breaks his word, and the man he runs at welcomes him.
screen: `KRISHNA CAME UNARMED` → `ARJUNA HOLDS BACK` → `THE DRIVER JUMPS DOWN`

segments.voice: Here's how it happens in Ganguli's telling. Duryodhana has accused Bhishma of going easy on the Pandavas, and the old man is stung. So he fights like fire. And Arjuna, facing the grandfather he grew up with, fights gently; he can't make himself strike hard. Krishna sees the Pandava army breaking. He drops the reins, jumps down, and rushes at Bhishma with his discus raised. Bhishma doesn't flinch. He stands his ground, bow in hand, and calls out a welcome. Come, strike me down. To be killed by you would be an honor. The enemy commander greets the attack with something close to joy. Then Arjuna jumps down after Krishna, grabs him, and holds on. He's dragged along the ground until Krishna finally stops. Arjuna begs him to turn back, and swears he'll fight in earnest. Krishna climbs back into the chariot. And it doesn't end there. Days later, it happens again. Bhishma is unstoppable, Arjuna is still too gentle, and Krishna leaps down once more, this time with nothing in his hand but his horse whip. Bhishma welcomes him again. Arjuna pulls him back again. Some later retellings add that Bhishma had sworn to make Krishna break his vow. Whatever you make of that, the scene in the text is plain enough. The teacher who told Arjuna to do his duty without wavering is pushed so far by his student's holding back that he nearly breaks his own word. And the man everyone is trying to stop is the one on the field who seems least afraid.
screen: `ARJUNA FIGHTS TOO GENTLY` · `KRISHNA RUNS AT BHISHMA` · `BHISHMA: COME, STRIKE ME DOWN` · then, large: `ARJUNA HOLDS HIM BACK, TWICE`

segments.voice: This week began with a man sitting down in his chariot and ends with a teacher jumping out of one. Look back over your own week: breathing in, find one moment you held back; breathing out, one moment you moved, and let them sit side by side without judging either. If you pray, you can offer both.
